forces.title: Ambitious 500 GW renewable capacity target by 2030
forces.description: India has significantly increased its renewable energy target to 500 GW by 2030, with a substantial portion (280 GW) expected from solar power. This ambitious national goal, backed by government commitment to decarbonization and energy security, creates a strong and sustained demand for utility-scale renewable power generation projects, driving policy support, investment, and infrastructure development across the country.

forces.title: Robust government policy and increased budget support for renewables
forces.description: The Indian government demonstrates strong policy backing for renewables through increased budget allocations for the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (40.52% rise in FY27), schemes like PM-KUSUM and SHP Development, and the National Electricity Policy 2026 emphasizing large-scale RE integration. A liberal 100% FDI policy for the sector further encourages foreign investment. This comprehensive support framework de-risks investments and accelerates project development for grid-connected renewable generators.

forces.title: Growing FDI and private sector investment in clean energy
forces.description: India's renewable energy sector is attracting significant foreign direct investment, with RE's share in total FDI inflows growing from 1% in FY21 to 8% in FY25, amounting to over US$ 23 billion cumulative. Major Indian conglomerates like ReNew Energy, NTPC, and JSW Neo Energy are also committing billions to hybrid and solar/wind projects. This influx of capital signals strong investor confidence and provides essential funding for grid-connected renewable capacity expansion.

forces.title: Rapidly rising electricity demand fuels renewable energy growth
forces.description: India faces surging electricity demand driven by population growth, widespread electrification, and increased industrial/residential consumption, with peak demand reaching 250 GW in May 2024 and projected to hit 458 GW by FY32. This growing load strengthens the investment case for renewables, allowing new wind and solar projects to meet incremental demand without displacing existing assets, thereby improving project economics for grid-connected generators.

forces.title: Traditional power producers diversifying into non-conventional energy
forces.description: India's leading conventional energy producers, such as Coal India Limited and NTPC, are increasingly shifting towards non-conventional energy resources and forming joint ventures to develop renewable energy projects. This strategic diversification is driven by sustainability goals, decarbonization targets, and the long-term shift in energy policy. This structural change brings significant capital, expertise, and procurement power into the grid-connected renewable sector, fostering its growth and integration.

forces.title: Systemic flexibility solutions crucial for maximizing RE value
forces.description: BCG emphasizes that systemic flexibility, involving smarter management of electricity consumption, storage, and movement, is critical to overcome value cannibalization in renewable-dominated grids. Solutions like Battery Energy Storage Systems, smart consumption tools, and redesigned markets that reward quick responses and duration will enable higher RE penetration while ensuring grid stability and producer revenues. This shift from capacity-centric to value-centric planning offers significant upside for grid-connected renewables.

forces.title: Value cannibalization and price volatility threaten RE investments
forces.description: As renewable energy penetration increases, oversupply during high generation periods depresses wholesale electricity prices, leading to 'value cannibalization.' This phenomenon reduces producer revenues, increases market volatility, and poses a risk that investments in renewable energy could diminish. This is a significant headwind, requiring market redesigns and flexibility solutions to maintain the financial attractiveness and profitability of grid-connected renewable projects globally.

forces.title: Grid bottlenecks and curtailment challenge renewable integration
forces.description: Insufficient grid capacity and bottlenecks reduce the value of renewable energy, particularly in areas of oversupply, leading to forced curtailment of generation. This causes revenue losses for renewable energy producers and can even result in negative energy prices. Expanding and modernizing power grids are imperative to efficiently transmit power from generation sites to demand centers, thereby mitigating this key headwind for grid-connected renewables and ensuring optimal utilization of assets.

forces.title: Non-resource specific factors gaining importance for RE scaling
forces.description: Beyond natural resource availability, factors like affordable land, existing renewable infrastructure, robust grid connectivity, and strong local power demand growth are increasingly becoming decisive for scaling renewable energy projects. This structural shift means that policy and planning efforts need to focus on optimizing these enablers, such as reducing land costs and investing in utility infrastructure, to attract and sustain grid-connected renewable development and ensure their economic viability.

forces.title: Development of hybrid renewable projects with storage solutions
forces.description: The increasing focus on hybrid renewable projects (wind-solar) coupled with battery energy storage systems and pumped hydro storage addresses the intermittent nature of standalone solar/wind. These projects, exemplified by ReNew Energy's 5 GW hybrid investments and NLC India's wind-solar hybrid projects with 25-year PPAs, provide round-the-clock power, enhance grid stability, and maximize the value of renewable generation, offering a significant upside for the grid-connected renewable power generation sector.

forces.title: Elevated long-term interest rates increase project financing costs
forces.description: Higher long-term interest rates, relative to the early 2020s, are keeping financing costs elevated for capital-intensive power projects, including grid-connected renewables. This macroeconomic dynamic, coupled with geopolitical volatility, materially impacts the economics of renewable projects which are highly sensitive to the cost of capital. This represents a significant key risk that can deter new investments, reduce project internal rates of return, and affect overall profitability in the sector.

viewpoints.title: Non-resource factors crucial for scaling renewables globally
viewpoints.description: BCG's analysis reveals that non-resource specific factors, such as affordable land, existing renewable capacity base, robust grid infrastructure, and power demand growth, are more critical for successful renewable energy scaling than resource abundance. This implies that strategic infrastructure investment and conducive policy environments are paramount to accelerating renewable deployment. Policymakers should focus on reducing land costs and attracting transmission investments to foster growth in grid-connected renewables.

viewpoints.title: Systemic flexibility vital for renewable energy financial viability
viewpoints.description: BCG argues that systemic flexibility is paramount for the future value and financial viability of renewable energy investments. As renewables become abundant, they risk cannibalizing their own value through price depression and volatility. Addressing this requires managing electricity consumption, storage, and movement across all timeframes. Ignoring flexibility risks drying up future investments, making it a critical aspect for sustainable growth in grid-connected renewable power generation.

viewpoints.title: India's renewable sector poised for robust growth and investment
viewpoints.description: IBEF highlights India's immense growth potential in renewable energy, particularly solar and wind, driven by ambitious targets (500 GW by 2030) and strong government support. Increased budget allocations for the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, liberal FDI policies, and significant investment plans by conglomerates underscore a positive outlook. The country's progress in surpassing climate targets and becoming a major global player reinforces this optimistic trajectory for grid-connected renewables.

demand_drivers.description: India's commitment to reducing carbon intensity by less than 45% by end of decade and achieving net-zero emissions by 2070.
Reducing reliance on fossil fuels and meeting rising energy demand through domestic renewable sources.

market_sizing.methodology: Government of India's ambitious target for cumulative installed non-fossil fuel electricity capacity by 2030, with 280 GW specifically expected from solar power.
Moody's estimate for the investment required in India to achieve the target of 500 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030. This figure specifically addresses the generation capacity component.

new_opportunities.description: Significant potential of 750 GW, including 3,343.37 GWp from ground-mounted PV on wasteland, indicating vast unexplored areas for project development.
Substantial untapped potential in wind (102 GW) and small hydro (20 GW) for further grid-connected renewable projects.

market_sizing.methodology: Estimated total renewable energy potential from commercially exploitable sources in India, including solar (750 GW), wind (102 GW), bio-energy (25 GW), and small hydro (20 GW).
ICRA's forecast for renewable capacity addition in India for 2025, representing an increase from 28 GW added in 2024.

demand_drivers.description: The Solar Park Scheme facilitates large-scale deployment of solar power projects by providing necessary infrastructure and support.

market_sizing.methodology: Total capacity sanctioned across 55 solar parks in 13 states as of February 2025. This figure indicates the substantial pipeline for utility-scale solar PV development projects in India.

demand_drivers.description: Increased outlays towards schemes like PM Surya Ghar and enhanced support for solar deployment, energy storage, and domestic manufacturing.
